## About these questions {.unnumbered}

These questions are for extra practice after Lab 6, using the same data.
Tasks 1–4 follow on from Task 1 of the lab (temperature), and Tasks 5 and 6 from Task 2 of the lab (rainfall).
Questions marked **Extension** are more challenging.

The cell below loads the weather data, and recreates the annual mean maximum temperatures for Southampton, Oxford, Sheffield and Paisley from Task 1 of the lab.

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
met <- read_csv("data/MET Office Weather Data.csv")
met <- met |>
    mutate(date = make_date(year, month, 1))

stations <- c("southampton", "oxford", "sheffield", "paisley")
annual <- met |>
    filter(station %in% stations) |>
    group_by(station, year) |>
    summarise(
        mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
        n_months = sum(!is.na(tmax)),
        .groups = "drop"
    )
```

### Task 1: Themes and Legends

- [ ] Experiment with different *themes* for your plot of July maximum temperatures in Southampton: how does it change if you use `theme_minimal()`, `theme_bw()`?
- [ ] In your scatter plot of monthly maximum temperatures at four stations, adjust the theme to move the legend to the bottom of the plot. (Hint: look for `legend.position` in the help page for `theme`.)

::: {.solution}

Themes are added like any other layer:

```{r}
met |>
    filter(station == "southampton" & month == 7) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = tmax)) +
    geom_line() +
    labs(
        x = "Date",
        y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "July maximum temperatures in Southampton"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
```

A theme changes only the *non-data* parts of the plot: the background, gridlines, borders and fonts.
The line itself, the axes and the scales are unchanged.
The default theme (`theme_grey()`) has a grey background with white gridlines; `theme_minimal()` removes the background and border, and `theme_bw()` uses a white background with a black border.
The lighter themes often work better in reports and when printed.

The legend position is also part of the theme, so we change it with `theme()`:

```{r}
met |>
    filter(station %in% stations) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = tmax, colour = station)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_smooth() +
    labs(
        x = "Date",
        y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "Monthly maximum temperatures"
    ) +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

With the legend at the bottom, the plot itself can use the full width of the page.

:::

### Task 2: The Seasonal Cycle and Facets

- [ ] Plot `tmax` against `month` for Southampton. How large is the seasonal swing in temperature, compared with the change in the smooth lines in your scatter plot of monthly maximum temperatures?
- [ ] Use `facet_wrap` to produce the scatter plot with smooth trend lines for all stations (not just the four in the lab). Does this support your conclusion about the trend in maximum temperatures?
- [ ] Adjust output options to make the plot more visible: modify the `ncol` option of `facet_wrap`, and adjust the rendered plot size by adding a `#| fig-height:` option to the top of the cell (in the same way as `#| message: false`).
- [ ] **Extension:** Produce the annual-mean plot (complete years only) for all 36 stations using `facet_wrap`, and compare it with your faceted plot of monthly values. Does it now support the conclusion that temperatures are rising?

::: {.solution}

Plotting against `month` shows the seasonal cycle:

```{r}
met |>
    filter(station == "southampton") |>
    ggplot(aes(x = month, y = tmax)) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
    labs(
        x = "Month",
        y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "Monthly maximum temperatures in Southampton"
    )
```

Mean maximum temperatures in Southampton range from about 7.5°C in January to about 22°C in July, a swing of roughly 14°C.
The smooth lines in the scatter plot changed by only a degree or so over the whole record, so the seasonal cycle completely dominates that plot.

The same scatter plot for all stations:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 8
met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = tmax)) +
    facet_wrap(~station, ncol = 4) +
    geom_point(alpha = 0.2) +
    geom_smooth() +
    labs(
        x = "Date",
        y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "Monthly maximum temperatures"
    )
```

This is consistent with the four-station plot: at most stations the smooth line creeps upwards, and at none does it clearly fall.
However, the plot does not really *confirm* a trend.
Each panel has to cover the whole seasonal range of temperatures, so a change of a degree or so is barely visible.

For the extension, we compute the annual means for every station, keep only complete years, and facet:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 8
met |>
    group_by(station, year) |>
    summarise(
        mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
        n_months = sum(!is.na(tmax)),
        .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    filter(n_months == 12) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax)) +
    facet_wrap(~station, ncol = 4) +
    geom_line() +
    geom_smooth() +
    labs(
        x = "Year",
        y = "Annual mean maximum temperature (°C)",
        title = "Annual mean maximum temperatures (complete years only)"
    )
```

Now a rise is visible at most stations, especially over the last few decades, which the faceted plot of monthly values could not show.

:::

### Task 3: Colour Blindness

- [ ] Redraw your plot of annual mean maximum temperatures (complete years only) from the lab so that it would still work for a reader with red–green colour blindness, or if printed in black and white. (Hint: see the Colour Blindness section of the Week 6 notes.)

::: {.solution}
The default colours are hard to tell apart for a reader with red–green colour blindness, and impossible to distinguish in black and white.
We can fix this by using a colourblind-safe palette (`viridis`), and by adding a *redundant* encoding, so that the plot does not rely on colour alone.
For points, the notes use `shape`; for lines, the equivalent is `linetype`.
Mapping `station` to both `colour` and `linetype` means each station differs in both.
We give both the same legend title in `labs`, so that `ggplot` combines them into a single legend:

```{r}
annual |>
    filter(n_months == 12) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, colour = station, linetype = station)) +
    geom_line(alpha = 0.4) +
    geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
    scale_colour_viridis_d() +
    labs(
        x = "Year",
        y = "Annual mean maximum temperature (°C)",
        colour = "Station",
        linetype = "Station",
        title = "Annual mean maximum temperatures (complete years only)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

With four overlapping line types the raw annual values become cluttered, so we have made them fainter with `alpha`, and removed the confidence bands (`se = FALSE`) so that the smooth trend lines stand out.
We also switched to `theme_minimal()`: the yellow end of the `viridis` palette is hard to see against the default grey background.
Note that `theme(legend.position = "bottom")` comes *after* `theme_minimal()`; a complete theme like `theme_minimal()` resets all theme settings, so it would undo the legend position if it came afterwards.

:::

### Task 4: Temperature and Sunshine

- [ ] Create a scatter plot of `tmax` against `date` across all stations. Colour the points by the amount of `sun` at that station.
- [ ] Look up the function `scale_colour_gradient2`. Use it to add a diverging colour scale, with low sun coloured blue, high sun coloured red. Set the midpoint to be the median value and the mid colour to be white.
- [ ] What conclusion can you draw from this plot?

::: {.solution}
```{r}
met |>
    filter(!is.na(sun)) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = date, y = tmax, colour = sun)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_colour_gradient2(
        low = "blue",
        mid = "white",
        high = "red",
        midpoint = median(met$sun, na.rm = TRUE)
    ) +
    labs(
        x = "Date",
        y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
        colour = "Sunshine (hours)",
        title = "Monthly maximum temperatures and sunshine"
    )
```

Higher temperatures are typically associated with more sunlight: the red (sunny) points are concentrated at the top of the plot, and the blue points at the bottom.
This does not necessarily mean the sun is *causing* the higher temperatures, though. Both are strongly related to the season: summer months are both sunnier and warmer than winter months.
:::

### Task 5: Comparing Stations

- [ ] Look at your bar chart of the number of monthly records at each station. Which stations have the longest records? How might this affect comparisons between stations, such as the average rainfall?

::: {.solution}

Armagh and Oxford have the longest records (2,010 rows each, going back to 1853), while Camborne has the shortest (502 rows, from 1978).
This means that an average over "all months and years" covers different periods at different stations.
If the climate has changed over time, the comparison is not like for like.
We saw in Task 1 of the lab that temperatures have risen, so a station with only a recent record would look warmer for that reason alone.
(For rainfall the effect appears to be small: for example, Oxford's mean monthly rainfall is about 55 mm both before and after 1959.)

Note also that these are counts of *rows*, not of measurements.
The count includes rows where `rain` is `NA`: at Ballypatrick, for example, 331 of the 709 rows have no rainfall value.

:::

### Task 6: More Distributions

- [ ] Customise your box plot of rainfall by station: change the length of the whiskers so that outliers appear at both the low and high ends, and change the outlier point colour to red. Does it make sense to call these points "outliers"?
- [ ] Look up how to flip the $x$ and $y$ axes, so that the rainfall appears on the $x$ axis and the station on the $y$ axis. (Hint: you can change the `aes`, but there is another way of doing it that doesn't require modifying the labels...)
- [ ] For a handful of stations (e.g. Southampton, Cwmystwyth, Eskdalemuir and Cambridge), overlay a violin plot and a narrow box plot, as in the Week 6 notes. What does the violin show that the box plot doesn't?
- [ ] **Extension:** Add a density curve on top of your histogram of monthly rainfall. (Hint: see the Week 6 notes.)

::: {.solution}

The whisker length is controlled by `coef`: the whiskers extend up to `coef` times the interquartile range (IQR) beyond the box, and points outside them are drawn as outliers.

```{r}
met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = rain)) +
    # coef determines how many times the interquartile range the whiskers extend from the box.
    geom_boxplot(outlier.colour = "red", outlier.size = 1, coef = 0.5) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Rainfall (mm)",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall by station"
    )
```

Reducing `coef` from its default of 1.5 to 0.5 shortens the whiskers, so that points at both ends are drawn as outliers.
Note that this is a display choice: it changes which points are *drawn* as outliers, not anything about the data.
With `coef = 0.5` over 5,000 months are marked as outliers, so they are hardly unusual.

To flip the axes, we can swap `x` and `y` in the `aes` (and the labels to match):

```{r}
met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = rain, y = station)) +
    # coef determines how many times the interquartile range the whiskers extend from the box.
    geom_boxplot(outlier.colour = "red", outlier.size = 1, coef = 0.5) +
    labs(
        y = "Station",
        x = "Rainfall (mm)",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall by station"
    )
```

Alternatively, we can keep the original code and add `coord_flip()`, which flips the coordinate system after everything else has been drawn.
The labels do not need to change, because they are still attached to the original `x` and `y` aesthetics.
Both approaches give the same plot:

```{r}
met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = rain)) +
    # coef determines how many times the interquartile range the whiskers extend from the box.
    geom_boxplot(outlier.colour = "red", outlier.size = 1, coef = 0.5) +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Rainfall (mm)",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall by station"
    ) +
    coord_flip()
```

For the violin plot, we filter to the chosen stations and add the two geometries as layers.
Setting `width = 0.15` makes the box plot narrow enough to sit inside the violin, and `outlier.shape = NA` hides the box plot's outliers, since the violin already shows the tails:

```{r}
met |>
    filter(station %in% c("southampton", "cwmystwyth", "eskdalemuir", "cambridge")) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = station, y = rain)) +
    geom_violin() +
    geom_boxplot(width = 0.15, outlier.shape = NA) +
    labs(
        x = "Station",
        y = "Monthly rainfall (mm)",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall at four stations"
    )
```

The box plot summarises each distribution with five numbers, while the violin shows its full *shape*: where the values are concentrated and how quickly they thin out.
Here it shows that every station is right-skewed, with a long, thin tail of wet months.
It also shows that at the drier stations (Cambridge and Southampton) most months are packed closely together at around 40 mm, while at the wetter stations (Cwmystwyth and Eskdalemuir) the rainfall is much more spread out.

For the extension, we rescale the histogram to a density with `after_stat(density)`, so that it is on the same scale as the density curve:

```{r}
met |>
    ggplot(aes(x = rain)) +
    geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 50) +
    geom_density(linewidth = 1) +
    labs(
        x = "Monthly rainfall (mm)",
        y = "Density",
        title = "Distribution of monthly rainfall across all stations"
    )
```

:::
